solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Far right Conservative is in sexually promiscuous embrace

indicators.note: to embrace is to wrap your arms around, so one piece wraps around the others

parts.note: a fast person, in the old phrase, is loose in morals
C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative
taken as written

explanation.surface: A right-wing Tory caught up in a sex scandal, in typical Private Eye style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Far right Conservative' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at 'Far right'; the Conservative is just a letter tucked inside, with 'is', between the last two letters of the promiscuous word.
explanation.definitionFit: Fascism sits at the extreme authoritarian end of politics, so a far-right person is commonly labelled with this noun.

clue.text: Didn't vote for awful British leaders — smeared

indicators.note: leaders go in front, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

parts.note: the opening letters of these two words
something smeared is marked or stained

explanation.surface: A voter refusing to back a dreadful set of British politicians who have been tarnished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awful British leaders' looks like a jibe at the government, but 'leaders' just picks the first letter of each of the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstain is to decline formally to cast a ballot, so the past tense matches someone who did not vote.

clue.text: 'Intercourse' joint, dockyard town

parts.note: intercourse in its older sense of conversation
a ham is a joint of meat

explanation.surface: It sounds like a seedy venue for sex, a 'joint' where intercourse happens, in some naval port.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks flag that 'intercourse' is not sexual here: it means conversation. Chatham is a town in Kent, home for centuries to a Royal Navy dockyard.
explanation.definitionFit: Chatham in Kent was the site of a major Royal Navy dockyard from Tudor times until 1984, hence its description.

clue.text: Try to put a good light on annexing a country

indicators.note: to annex territory is to take it inside your own borders, so one piece absorbs another

parts.words: Try to put a good light on
parts.note: spin is presenting news in the most favourable way
taken as written

explanation.surface: A spin doctor trying to make the seizure of another nation look respectable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Annexing a country' reads as one political act, but the 'a' is a letter being taken in while 'a country' is also the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Spain is an example of a nation state, the Iberian kingdom whose capital is Madrid.

clue.text: Prune gets union affiliation to do a U-turn and take a gamble

indicators.note: a U-turn sends you back the way you came, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: the Trades Union Congress, Britain's federation of trade unions
to back a horse is to bet on it

explanation.surface: A leader trimming policy so the unions reverse their stance, then rolling the dice.
explanation.walkthrough: The TUC is the Trades Union Congress, the body British unions affiliate to.
explanation.definitionFit: To prune a plant is to trim away branches, and this phrasal verb also means reducing spending or growth.

clue.text: Lack of interest in body that's very large and firm

parts.note: the United Nations, a very large international body
a concern is a business

explanation.surface: Someone unmoved by a hugely fat, toned physique.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very large and firm' paints a body, but 'firm' is a noun, a business, and 'body' is an organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: Unconcern is indifference, a state of not caring or feeling curious about something.

clue.text: Nonconformist Family Bill put up to confine English

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting something up means writing it from bottom to top

parts.note: kin are relatives

indicators.note: confining something shuts it inside, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: a tab is a bill, as in a bar tab
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A dissenting chapel's family legislation proposed to restrict English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nonconformist' suggests a chapel denomination, but here it simply means a rebel. The bill encloses the E, follows the family, and the whole string is read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Beatniks of the 1950s rejected mainstream values and dress, making them the archetypal social rebels.

clue.text: Acid distributed by unknown port

indicators.note: distributed things are spread about, so these letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
in algebra x, y and z are unknowns

explanation.surface: LSD being handed out by a mysterious dealer at the docks.
explanation.walkthrough: Z is one of the letters mathematicians use for an unknown quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: Cádiz is an ancient Andalusian harbour city on Spain's Atlantic coast, long a major naval and trading base.

clue.text: Commons and Lords leaders cite bad language

indicators.note: something bad is spoilt or wrong, so these letters are messed up into another order
leaders go in front, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

parts.note: the opening letters of the two Houses
taken as written

explanation.surface: Heads of both Houses of Parliament quoting swear words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad language' looks like swearing, but 'bad' is the anagram signal and 'language' alone is the definition; the two initials join the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Celtic is the branch of Indo-European speech including Welsh, Irish and Scottish Gaelic, Breton and Cornish.

clue.text: Fly opened by perverse prosecutor for a romp

indicators.note: something opened up has another thing put inside it

parts.note: to fly is to flee or get away

indicators.note: perverse means turned the wrong way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a district attorney, the American public prosecutor

explanation.surface: A kinky lawyer undoing a trouser zip in pursuit of some fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' looks like a trouser zip but is the verb to flee. DA is the American district attorney.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapade is an adventurous, often mischievous exploit, much like a romp or a frolic.

clue.text: About having an erection, which might be pulled in the vegetable garden

definitions.text: which might be pulled in the vegetable garden
definitions.note: a descriptive clause standing for the noun

parts.note: c. is short for circa, about
slang for being sexually aroused

explanation.surface: A smutty joke about something being pulled while aroused, until the garden turns up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulled' is set up as innuendo, but the clause simply describes a leaf vegetable picked by tugging off its stems.
explanation.definitionFit: Swiss chard is a leafy plot vegetable whose stalks are commonly harvested by pulling them from the plant.

clue.text: President's dirty laundry not to be broadcast!

parts.note: the clothes waiting to be laundered

indicators.note: broadcasting scatters something widely, like seed flung across a field, so the letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A warning that a president's scandals, his dirty laundry, must never be aired in public.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface leans on the idiom about not airing dirty laundry in public, but 'broadcast' only scrambles the three-letter word before it; the apostrophe-s stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: George Washington was the first holder of the American presidency, so his surname fits a president by example.

clue.text: (& 27ac.) New: A Life as a Painter — Hitler's Lot

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
taken as written
zip means energy or vitality, life in the sense of liveliness
arty means artistic, as a painter might be

explanation.surface: It reads like the title of a new biography of Hitler's early years as a would-be artist.
explanation.walkthrough: Hitler really did try to make a living as a painter before politics, which is why the surface works as a book title; 'Life' means liveliness, not biography.
explanation.definitionFit: The National Socialist German Workers' Party was the political organisation Hitler led, so his 'lot' is that crowd of followers.

clue.text: Coming out — like our proprietor?

definitions.note: the question mark flags a punning reading of the adjective

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or not in place, so the letters are shifted into another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A hint that the magazine's owner is about to come out as gay.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye's fictional proprietor is Lord Gnome, so 'like our proprietor' is read as gnome-like; the word really means cryptic and pithy, which also fits the paper's style.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective normally means expressed in short, enigmatic sayings, but here it is punningly read as resembling Lord Gnome.

clue.text: Stay calm, somehow, after pandemic's ultimate disaster

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters are rearranged in a way left for you to find

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: ultimate means last, so only the closing letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: Advice to keep calm after the final catastrophe of a pandemic.
explanation.walkthrough: The added letter joins the shuffle; 'after' only says where it sits in the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A cataclysm is a sudden violent upheaval or catastrophe, so it is a stronger synonym for a calamity.

clue.text: see 23ac.
Drugs managed to turn round company jerks

indicators.note: turning round faces the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to run a business is to manage it
Co. is the abbreviation for company
tics are involuntary twitches

explanation.surface: Drugs are said to have helped turn around a firm full of idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerks' looks like an insult for fools, but it means sudden twitching movements.
explanation.definitionFit: Narcotics are drugs that dull the senses, and the word is used broadly for illegal substances.

clue.text: After a date, fool getting end away with Heath is hooked

indicators.note: sending the end away means its last letter is cut off

parts.note: taken as written
d. is the abbreviation for date
a dick is a fool; cut short
Ted Heath, Conservative British Prime Minister 1970 to 1974

explanation.surface: Smutty Private Eye innuendo: after a date, some idiot 'gets his end away' with the former Prime Minister and is besotted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting one's end away' is British slang for having sex, but here it means losing the last letter. Edward 'Ted' Heath was Britain's Conservative Prime Minister in the early 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: To be hooked on something is to be dependent on it, a slang synonym for compulsive dependency.

clue.text: "You, then us, then you .." said Monica Lewinsky and colleagues?

definitions.note: an example of the class, hence the question mark

indicators.note: something said is spoken, so what counts is how the words come out of the mouth

parts.note: taking it one after the other, alternately

explanation.surface: Monica Lewinsky and fellow staffers describing a rota, with a sly hint at Clinton.
explanation.walkthrough: Monica Lewinsky was a White House intern whose affair with Bill Clinton became a scandal, so the alternating quotation carries innuendo.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewinsky worked as an unpaid trainee at the White House, so she and fellow trainees exemplify the plural noun.

clue.text: Insensitive heartless bonk is fatal

indicators.note: without a heart means the central letter is taken out

parts.note: dead to something means unfeeling towards it
a lay is a sexual partner or act; its middle letter goes

explanation.surface: A cold, loveless bit of sex being called a killer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bonk' is British slang for sex, as is 'lay', which loses its middle letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Deadly and fatal are synonyms, both describing something capable of causing death.

clue.text: Lawyer? No thanks — right, end of story!

parts.note: taken as written
ta is British informal for thank you
R is the abbreviation for right

indicators.note: the end of a word is its closing letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone firmly turning down a lawyer: no thanks, right, that's the end of it.
explanation.walkthrough: Ta is everyday British for thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: A notary is a legal officer who certifies documents and witnesses signatures, a kind of solicitor.

clue.text: Anguish of Cyclops name being implicated in wrongdoing

indicators.note: to be implicated in something is to be caught up inside it

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law
the setter refers to himself, so his name stands for me
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: The setter fretting that his name has been dragged into a scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops is this puzzle's setter, so his name means 'me'. A tort is a civil wrong in law.
explanation.definitionFit: Torment and anguish are near synonyms for severe mental or physical suffering.

clue.text: (& 16ac.) Teaching KFC about suppressing carbon a full-time job these days?

definitions.note: a cryptic hint at an activity rather than a dictionary equivalent

indicators.note: to suppress something is to hold it down and keep it in
about can mean around in all directions, so the letters are turned every which way

parts.note: taken as written
C is the chemical symbol for carbon

explanation.surface: Wondering whether educating a fast-food chain on reducing its carbon emissions is now a career in itself.
explanation.walkthrough: KFC is the fried-chicken chain. The carbon letter is held within the other letters and then everything is jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: Verifying claims has become constant work in an age of misinformation, so the job is described as never-ending.

clue.text: Distinctive mark at centre of ritual phallus

indicators.note: the centre of a phrase lies within it, so the letters sit inside the words

parts.note: found inside the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: An ancient fertility symbol bearing a special mark.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans the end of the first word and the start of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: An alpha is the top grade given to excellent work, a mark that distinguishes the best.

clue.text: House of Lords possibly has reserve that's handy for a peer

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the noun

parts.note: the Lords is a parliamentary chamber
a pot is a fund of money set aside

explanation.surface: The Lords keeping a cash fund on hand for its members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' looks like a lord, but read as 'pee-er' it is someone who urinates.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedroom vessel for urine is useful to someone needing to relieve themselves, the pun on 'peer'.

clue.text: Singer with nothing on is game

parts.note: Bing Crosby, the American crooner
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: A naked singer is up for anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing on' suggests nudity; in a down entry 'on' puts the circle below the singer. 'Game' means willing in the surface but is the noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: Bingo is a numbers game of chance in which players mark off called numbers on cards.

clue.text: see 13ac.
Hang on, that is pants, and more!

parts.note: to hang on is to stay around
i.e. is the abbreviation for id est, that is

explanation.surface: Someone protesting that an idea is rubbish, and worse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' is British slang for rubbish, which is how the surface reads; here it means underpants.
explanation.definitionFit: Lingerie covers women's underwear generally: knickers plus bras, slips and other intimate garments.

clue.text: Wobbly ass and a tum that's segmented

definitions.note: a descriptive clause standing for the noun

indicators.note: something wobbly is unsteady and shaken about, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wobbly backside and belly divided into rolls of flab.
explanation.walkthrough: The defining clause describes the fruit, which falls into segments when peeled.
explanation.definitionFit: A satsuma is a small loose-skinned citrus fruit whose flesh divides into wedges like an orange.

clue.text: Dispute rip-off examination

parts.note: a con is a swindle
a test is an exam

explanation.surface: Challenging a test that was a swindle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dispute' can be read as a verb or a noun; the answer works both ways.
explanation.definitionFit: To contest a decision is to challenge or argue against it, a direct synonym.
